sub_answers.sub_question: What post-election legal challenges and court rulings related to Wisconsin's 2020 election procedures and results were filed and resolved?
sub_answers.text: The Trump campaign brought an unsuccessful case to overturn Wisconsin's 2020 presidential election results that the Wisconsin Supreme Court rejected, with Justice Rebecca Bradley issuing a dissent in that unsuccessful challenge [d47395645s6p0].

sub_answers.text: Claims of widespread electoral fraud and irregularities were made in the aftermath of the 2020 election, including by President Trump and others alleging improper counting or handling of ballots [d382165s11p0].

sub_answers.text: Wisconsin state officials proceeded with certification and legal processes despite controversy, and the Wisconsin Supreme Court issued rulings related to election procedure disputes during 2020 including striking down a postponement of an election and later resolving challenges to election procedures [d47395645s6p0].

sub_answers.text: Casting a ballot in person before the date of the election is considered an absentee vote in Wisconsin.[d47395645s6p0]  The Wisconsin Supreme Court struck down Governor Evers' order to postpone the April 7, 2020 election, allowing the election to proceed as scheduled.[d47395645s6p0]  Justice Rebecca Bradley voted in person on April 2, 2020 and the record shows she cast in-person Election Day ballots in four of the five previous elections, illustrating use of in-person and early-absentee voting methods by voters and officials.[d47395645s6p0]

sub_answers.text: Casting a ballot in person before the date of the election is legally treated as an absentee vote in Wisconsin.[d47395645s6p0]  The Wisconsin Supreme Court's decisions during 2020 affected whether scheduled elections proceeded or were postponed, thereby shaping how ballots were cast and opened for counting.[d47395645s6p0]  Justice Rebecca Bradley participated in court rulings that influenced election timing and procedures during the pandemic.[d47395645s6p0]

sub_answers.text: The Trump campaign brought an unsuccessful case seeking to overturn the 2020 presidential election results in Wisconsin.[d47395645s6p0]  A dissenting minority on the Wisconsin Supreme Court agreed with some of the campaign's allegations but did not specify corrective relief.[d47395645s6p0]  Justice Rebecca Bradley described the majority's decision not to overturn the election as causing significant harm to the rule of law in her dissent.[d47395645s6p0]

sub_answers.text:
The Wisconsin Supreme Court struck down Governor Evers' order to postpone the April 7, 2020, election, keeping the election schedule in place for 2020 mail-in and absentee processes [d47395645s6p0].
Wisconsin treats an in-person vote cast before Election Day as an absentee ballot under state practice, as evidenced by Justice Rebecca Bradley casting an in-person April 2 ballot that was considered absentee [d47395645s6p0].
In Teigen v. Wisconsin Election Commission, Justice Bradley wrote that ballot drop boxes are illegal under Wisconsin statutes, framing drop-box use as contrary to statutory text [d47395645s6p0].

Justice Rebecca Bradley voted in person on April 2, 2020, and that in-person early vote was treated as an absentee ballot under Wisconsin practice [d47395645s6p0].
Wisconsin election administration in 2020 was the subject of litigation reaching the state Supreme Court concerning the timing and procedures for elections during the COVID-19 pandemic [d47395645s6p0].
In the post-election litigation, Bradley joined other conservative justices in dissenting from the majority that refused to grant the Trump campaign's requested relief to overturn November 2020 presidential results in Wisconsin [d47395645s6p0].
